chief_complaint: heavy prolonged periods and pelvic pressure
hpi_details: A 23-year-old female presents to the clinic with heavy prolonged periods and pelvic pressure. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks the abnormal bleeding is caused by severe hormonal disruption from the stress of starting her new job.
concerns: She is worried that she might pass out from severe blood loss while commuting on the crowded train to work.
expectations: She hopes to receive medication to stop the heavy bleeding right away and prescription iron pills for her fatigue.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Uterine leiomyomas (fibroids) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Uterine Leiomyomas: Check CBC, transvaginal ultrasound, discuss hormonal vs myomectomy, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Uterine leiomyomas (fibroids).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Adenomyosis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Prolonged heavy bleeding.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with heavy prolonged periods, pelvic pressure, and fatigue; further history and examination are needed to identify the cause.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Uterine Leiomyomas.
reference_soap.assessment: Abnormal uterine bleeding with pelvic pressure; evaluate for leiomyomas and other structural, endocrine, and pregnancy-related causes.
reference_soap.plan: Assess hemodynamic stability, obtain a pregnancy test and CBC, and arrange pelvic ultrasound. Select medical or procedural management only after diagnosis, bleeding severity, fertility goals, and contraindications are established.

must_ask.say: How many days does your period last, and how heavy is it?
Have you felt fatigued or short of breath?
Do you feel a sense of fullness or pressure in your pelvis?
Would you prefer to try medication first, or are you interested in surgical options?
We'll check your blood count and arrange a pelvic ultrasound to look for fibroids or another cause of the bleeding.

history.answer: I came to the clinic because my periods have become unusually heavy and seem to drag on for days, and I've been feeling this heavy pressure in my lower pelvis.
My periods used to arrive regularly every 28 days like clockwork, but over the last three months the flow has become much heavier and the intervals feel shorter.
I have to change overnight maxi pads every one to two hours on my heaviest days, and I notice large dark jelly-like blood clots. It frequently leaks through onto my clothes at night.
My period used to last about five days, but this current cycle has been bleeding heavily for ten days straight and shows no sign of stopping.
No, I haven't missed any periods or gone months without one; if anything, the bleeding is starting earlier and lasting longer.
I haven't had spotty bleeding between cycles until this prolonged period started, and I haven't noticed bleeding right after intercourse.
I have felt noticeably exhausted, sluggish, and lightheaded when I stand up quickly, especially over the past week. I don't feel breathless at rest, but climbing stairs wipes me out.
I have a constant dull fullness and heaviness low in my pelvis that feels like a weight pressing down, but I wouldn't call it sharp cramping pain.
I feel like I need to urinate much more often than usual and always feel a sense of pressure on my bladder, but it doesn't burn when I pee. My bowel movements have been normal.
No, I haven't had any unusual acne breakouts, increased facial hair, or sudden weight gain.
No, I haven't felt unusually sensitive to heat or cold, and my heart doesn't feel like it's racing or fluttering.
No, I have never had any milky discharge from my breasts, nor have I suffered from headaches or changes in my vision.
My weight has been completely steady, and I haven't changed my diet or started intense workouts. Work has been normal with no extreme stress.
No, I don't get spontaneous nosebleeds or bleeding gums, and I don't bruise easily. My periods have never been this heavy in the past, even when I first started menstruating at age twelve.
I am not taking birth control pills, hormone patches, blood thinners, or psychiatric medications, and I have never had an IUD placed.
I am in a monogamous relationship and we use condoms consistently. There has been no unprotected sex recently.
I have never been pregnant and have never given birth. I do hope to have children in the future, which is why I want to make sure my uterus stays healthy.
I had my first Pap smear last year and the result was completely normal. I do not have diabetes, obesity, or long-standing skipped periods.
I was wondering if starting my new job and being under so much stress completely threw my hormones out of whack.
I have been feeling so dizzy and weak that I am terrified I might faint on the train during my morning commute.
I am hoping you can prescribe something to stop this heavy bleeding today and give me some strong iron pills to get my energy back.
I would strongly prefer medical treatments or minimally invasive options first to preserve my uterus for future pregnancies, rather than anything aggressive.
I have always been healthy and have never been diagnosed with high blood pressure, diabetes, thyroid disease, or any chronic illness.
I have never had any surgeries, procedures, or hospital admissions.
I am not taking any prescription medications, over-the-counter pain relievers, iron supplements, or herbal remedies.
I have no known allergies to any medications, foods, or materials.
I have never smoked cigarettes, e-cigarettes, or used any tobacco products.
I only drink alcohol socially on occasion, perhaps one glass of wine or beer a month.
I work as an administrative assistant at a logistics office, and I live in an apartment with my roommate.
My mother had uterine fibroids removed in her late thirties, but no one in my family has a history of bleeding disorders, uterine cancer, or ovarian cancer.
The first day of my current menstrual period was ten days ago, on September 20th, and I am still bleeding heavily today.
We use condoms reliably every single time, so pregnancy is extremely unlikely, though I am completely willing to take a pregnancy test today to confirm.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg, pulse is 82 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 16 breaths per minute, and body temperature is 36.8 degrees Celsius.
Mild conjunctival pallor is present bilaterally; sclerae are anicteric.
Thyroid gland is normal in size and texture, non-tender, with no palpable nodules.
No hirsutism, acne, acanthosis nigricans, petechiae, or unexplained bruises are observed on exposed skin.
Abdomen is flat and symmetric without visible distension, caput medusae, or surgical scars.
A firm, non-tender, mobile mass is palpated in the suprapubic midline extending just above the symphysis pubis; no guarding or rigidity.
No rebound tenderness is elicited in any quadrant.

Speculum exam demonstrates moderate dark bloody discharge from the cervical os without cervical friability or lesions; bimanual exam reveals an irregularly enlarged, mobile, non-tender uterus roughly the size of a 10-week gestation.
